novice.body: The two truth values. Comparisons produce them, and if-statements consume them. Capitalized — true and false are errors.

learning.body: The bool constants. Other values have truthiness too: empty containers, 0, and None count as false in conditions.

comfortable.body: bool subclasses int (True == 1), which enables sum(predicate(x) for x in xs) counting — and the occasional surprise.

gotcha: They must be capitalized: "true" is just an undefined name.

novice.body: Loops over a collection while also counting: each pass gives you the position and the item together.

learning.body: Wraps an iterable to yield (index, item) pairs — the Pythonic replacement for looping over range(len(x)). start= sets the first index.

comfortable.body: Lazy (index, item) iterator; pairs naturally with tuple unpacking in the for target.

example.code:
for i, letter in enumerate("abc"):
    print(i, letter)

gotcha: Each element is a pair — unpack it as "for i, item in ..." or you'll get tuples.

novice.body: Pauses the program and waits for the user to type something. Whatever they type comes back as text.

learning.body: Reads one line from the keyboard and returns it as a string — always a string, even if the user types a number. Convert with int() or float().

comfortable.body: Blocking read from stdin, newline stripped; raises EOFError at end of input.

gotcha: input always returns a string: input() + 1 is a TypeError until you convert it.

novice.body: Asks whether a value is a certain type: isinstance(3, int) is True.

learning.body: Type check that respects inheritance — an instance of a subclass counts. Accepts a tuple of types: isinstance(x, (int, float)).

comfortable.body: Prefer over type(x) == T for polymorphism; with abstract base classes it checks interfaces, not just ancestry.

gotcha: bool is a subclass of int — isinstance(True, int) is True, which surprises everyone once.

novice.body: Tells you how many items something holds — characters in a string, elements in a list, keys in a dictionary.

learning.body: Returns the item count of any sized container. It's a function, not a method: len(x), never x.len().

comfortable.body: Dispatches to __len__; O(1) for all built-in containers.

gotcha: len works on containers, not numbers — len(42) is a TypeError.

novice.body: The "nothing here" value. Functions that don't return anything actually return None, and it's often used to mean "no answer yet."

learning.body: The single null object. Test for it with "is None", not "== None". It's falsy, but so are 0 and "" — check identity when you specifically mean None.

comfortable.body: Singleton of NoneType; the conventional default-argument sentinel (def f(x=None)) precisely because of the mutable-default trap.

example.code:
result = print("hi")
print(result is None)  # True

gotcha: "if not x" is True for 0 and "" too — use "if x is None" when None is what you mean.

novice.body: Opens a file so your program can read or write it. Almost always used with "with", which closes the file for you.

learning.body: Returns a file object; the mode string picks reading ("r"), writing ("w" — erases!), or appending ("a"). Pair with with for guaranteed cleanup.

comfortable.body: Text mode decodes via encoding= (pass it explicitly; the default is platform-dependent pre-3.15); "b" modes yield bytes.

gotcha: Mode "w" truncates the file the moment it opens — before you've written anything.

novice.body: Shows a value on the screen. It's how your program talks to you — it doesn't change or return anything useful.

learning.body: Writes its arguments to standard output, separated by spaces, with a newline at the end. sep= and end= customize both.

comfortable.body: I/O side effect returning None; end="" suppresses the newline, file= redirects, flush=True forces immediate output.

gotcha: print returns None — capturing "x = print(5)" stores nothing useful.

novice.body: Produces a sequence of counting numbers, most often to run a loop N times. range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 — it stops before the number you give it.

learning.body: range(start, stop, step) counts from start up to (but not including) stop. It's lazy — wrap it in list() to see the numbers.

comfortable.body: A lazy immutable sequence with O(1) membership tests and slicing; not a generator — it can be iterated repeatedly.

gotcha: The stop value is never produced: range(1, 5) ends at 4.

novice.body: Gives back a new list with the items in order, smallest to largest. The original is left alone.

learning.body: Returns a new sorted list from any iterable. key= sorts by a computed value; reverse=True flips the order. list.sort() does the same in place.

comfortable.body: Timsort, stable — equal keys keep their relative order, which makes multi-pass sorts composable.

gotcha: sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.

novice.body: Adds up all the numbers in a collection: sum([1, 2, 3]) is 6.

learning.body: Totals any iterable of numbers; the second argument is a starting value. For joining strings use "".join() instead.

comfortable.body: Left fold with +; rejects str starts by design. math.fsum for float precision.

gotcha: sum on strings is blocked on purpose — use "".join(strings), which is far faster anyway.

novice.body: Walks two (or more) collections side by side, pairing up their items: first with first, second with second.

learning.body: Yields tuples of matched elements and stops at the shortest input. zip(*pairs) runs it in reverse to unzip.

comfortable.body: Lazy parallel iterator; strict=True (3.10+) raises on unequal lengths instead of silently truncating.

example.code:
names = ["Ada", "Alan"]
ages = [36, 41]
for name, age in zip(names, ages):
    print(name, age)

gotcha: zip silently stops at the shortest input — mismatched lengths lose data without warning.

novice.body: This line means "only run the code below when this file is run directly." When the file is imported by another file, the code below is skipped.

learning.body: Python sets the special variable __name__ to "__main__" when a file runs as the program, and to the module's name when it's imported. This check separates "script behavior" from "library behavior."

comfortable.body: The standard entry-point guard: run-time behavior lives here, importable definitions live above it. Keeps imports side-effect-free.

gotcha: Code above the guard still runs on import — only what's inside the if is protected.

novice.body: One equals sign stores the value on the right under the name on the left. It's an action, not a question — the question version is ==.

learning.body: Binds the name on the left to the value on the right.

comfortable.body: Name binding.

gotcha: Assigning a list to a second name doesn't copy it — both names point at the same list.

novice.body: Shorthand for "add to what's already there": count += 1 means count = count + 1.

learning.body: Augmented assignment; exists for most operators (-=, *=, //=). On lists, += extends in place rather than building a new list.

comfortable.body: Uses __iadd__ when available (in-place mutation) — which is why aug-assigning a list inside a tuple both mutates and raises.

gotcha: On mutable objects += changes the object in place — every other reference to it sees the change.

novice.body: Two equals signs ask a question — "are these the same value?" — and answer True or False. One equals sign stores a value instead.

learning.body: Value equality: compares contents, so [1, 2] == [1, 2] is True even for two separate lists. "is" checks identity (same object), which is different.

comfortable.body: Dispatches to __eq__. Use == for values, "is" only for None and sentinels.

gotcha: Writing = where you meant == inside a condition is a syntax error in Python — a helpful one.

novice.body: Division that throws away the remainder: 7 // 2 is 3. A single slash would give 3.5.

learning.body: Divides and rounds down (floor). With negatives it keeps rounding down: -7 // 2 is -4, not -3.

comfortable.body: Floor division, paired with % so that (a // b) * b + a % b == a. Rounds toward negative infinity, unlike C's truncation.

gotcha: It floors, not truncates: -7 // 2 is -4.

novice.body: Asks whether something is inside a collection: "a" in "cat" is True, 5 in [1, 2, 3] is False.

learning.body: Membership test for sequences, sets, and dicts (checks keys). "not in" is the negation. This is a different "in" from the one in a for loop.

comfortable.body: Dispatches to __contains__; O(1) for sets/dicts, O(n) for lists — the classic reason to convert a lookup list to a set.

gotcha: On a dict, "in" checks keys only — values need "x in d.values()".

novice.body: Gives the remainder after division: 7 % 2 is 1. Handy for "is this number even?" — n % 2 == 0.

learning.body: Remainder operator; the result takes the sign of the divisor, so -7 % 3 is 2 in Python. Common for wrapping indexes and even/odd checks.

comfortable.body: Modulo consistent with floor division. On strings it's legacy printf-style formatting — prefer f-strings.

gotcha: Sign follows the divisor: -7 % 3 is 2, not -1 — different from many other languages.

novice.body: Raises to a power: 2 ** 3 is 8. Not the same as 2 * 3.

learning.body: Exponentiation; works with fractional exponents too, so x ** 0.5 is a square root.

comfortable.body: Right-associative (2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512) and binds tighter than unary minus: -2 ** 2 is -4.

gotcha: -2 ** 2 is -4, because ** binds before the minus. Use (-2) ** 2 for 4.

novice.body: class defines a blueprint for objects: what data they carry and what they can do. Calling the class like a function — Dog("Rex") — builds a new object from the blueprint.

learning.body: Bundles data (attributes) with behavior (methods). Parentheses after the name declare a parent class to inherit from.

comfortable.body: The class body executes top-to-bottom at definition time in its own namespace; assignments there become class attributes shared by all instances.

gotcha: Attributes assigned in the class body (not in __init__) are shared by every instance.

novice.body: The @name line above a function wraps that function in extra behavior — the function below gets handed to the decorator, which can change or extend what it does.

learning.body: Syntax sugar: "@deco" above "def f" means f = deco(f). The decorator receives the function and returns a (usually enhanced) replacement.

comfortable.body: Function transformation applied at definition time. Decorators with arguments are factories: @deco(arg) calls deco(arg) first, then applies the result.

gotcha: Decorators run at definition time, not call time — side effects happen on import.

novice.body: Like a list comprehension, but it builds a dictionary: each pass produces a key and a value, written as key: value before the "for".

learning.body: Builds a dict from an iterable in one expression. Handy for inverting mappings or reshaping data: {k: v for k, v in pairs}.

comfortable.body: Dict construction with the comprehension syntax; later keys silently overwrite earlier duplicates.

example.code:
squares = {n: n * n for n in range(4)}
# {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9}

gotcha: Duplicate keys don't error — the last one quietly wins.

novice.body: The setup method of a class. It runs automatically every time a new object is created, and it's where the object's starting data gets attached with self.

learning.body: The initializer: Dog("Rex") creates the object, then calls __init__(self, "Rex") on it. Arguments to the class call become arguments to __init__.

comfortable.body: Initializes an already-created instance (__new__ does the creating). Should assign state and return None — returning anything else raises.

gotcha: It's spelled with two underscores on each side — "dunder init," not "_init_".

novice.body: Short for "else if" — another condition to try when the ones above it were false. Only the first true branch in the chain runs.

learning.body: Chains mutually exclusive conditions without nesting. Order matters: conditions are tested top to bottom and the rest are skipped after a hit.

comfortable.body: Flat alternative to nested else/if; for many branches on one value, match/case may read better.

gotcha: Exactly one branch runs — even if several conditions would have been true.

novice.body: A string that can contain live values: anything inside {curly braces} is Python code whose result gets inserted into the text.

learning.body: Formatted string literal — the f prefix makes {expressions} evaluate in place. Supports format specs after a colon, like {price:.2f} for two decimals.

comfortable.body: Compile-time interpolation; {expr!r} for repr, {expr=} to print the expression and its value — useful for quick debugging.

gotcha: Forget the f prefix and the braces print literally: "hello, {name}!".

novice.body: Repeats the indented block once for each item in a collection, putting the current item in the loop variable each time around.

learning.body: Iterates over anything iterable — lists, strings, files, dicts (their keys). Use enumerate() when you also need the index, and range() for plain counting.

comfortable.body: Drives the iterator protocol (iter/next). The optional else clause runs only if the loop completed without break.

gotcha: Looping over a dict gives you its keys, not key–value pairs — use .items() for both.

novice.body: Pulls specific names out of a module so you can use them directly: after "from math import sqrt", you write sqrt(9) with no prefix.

learning.body: Imports the whole module but binds only the listed names locally. Clearer than import-star, which dumps everything into your namespace.

comfortable.body: Binds by value at import time: "from config import DEBUG" won't see later reassignments of config.DEBUG.

gotcha: "from module import *" makes it impossible to tell where a name came from — avoid it.

novice.body: def creates a reusable named block of code. The names in parentheses are inputs; "return" sends a result back out. Nothing runs until the function is called.

learning.body: Defines a function object and binds it to the name. Parameters can have defaults (x=0); the body runs only on call, in its own local scope.

comfortable.body: Definition is execution: the def statement runs at import time, evaluating defaults once (hence the mutable-default trap).

gotcha: Default values are evaluated once at definition — a mutable default like def f(x=[]) is shared across calls.

novice.body: Looks like a list comprehension with round brackets, but it doesn't build the whole list — it produces items one at a time, as they're asked for.

learning.body: A lazy comprehension: nothing is computed until something iterates over it. Great for big or infinite sequences because it uses almost no memory.

comfortable.body: Lazy single-pass iterator. Once consumed it's exhausted — iterate twice and the second pass sees nothing.

example.code: total = sum(n * n for n in range(1000))

gotcha: A generator can be consumed only once; a second loop over it gets zero items.

novice.body: Loads another module so you can use its contents, accessed with a dot: after "import math", you write math.sqrt(9).

learning.body: Runs the module once (results are cached) and binds its name here. "import x as y" renames it locally.

comfortable.body: Module executes top-to-bottom on first import, then comes from sys.modules. Import-time side effects live in that first run.

gotcha: Importing runs the module's top-level code — that's why the __main__ guard exists.

novice.body: A double star collects extra name=value arguments into a dictionary (in a def), or spreads a dictionary out into name=value arguments (in a call).

learning.body: def f(**kwargs) gathers unexpected keyword arguments into a dict; f(**options) unpacks a dict as keyword arguments. Often used to pass options through to another function.

comfortable.body: Keyword packing/unpacking; also dict merging: {**a, **b} (last key wins). Order in signatures: positional, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs.

gotcha: Keys must be valid identifiers when unpacking into a call — {"my-key": 1} can't become a keyword argument.

novice.body: A tiny unnamed function written in one expression. "lambda x: x * 2" means the same as a def that takes x and returns x * 2.

learning.body: An inline function limited to a single expression, usually passed straight into something like sorted(key=...) or map().

comfortable.body: Single-expression closure. If it needs a name or a second line, make it a def.

gotcha: No statements allowed inside — no assignments, no loops, just one expression.

novice.body: A one-line way to build a new list from an existing one. Read it inside-out: "for n in numbers" walks the list, and the part before "for" says what to keep.

learning.body: Builds a list by transforming (and optionally filtering, with a trailing "if") each element of an iterable. Equivalent to a for-loop that appends, but shorter and usually faster.

comfortable.body: Eager list construction from an iterable; add "if" clauses to filter. Prefer a plain loop once it stops fitting on one readable line.

example.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
doubled = [n * 2 for n in numbers]  # [2, 4, 6]

gotcha: With parentheses instead of brackets you get a generator, not a list.

novice.body: Ends the function immediately and sends a value back to whoever called it. Code after the return never runs.

learning.body: Exits with a result; "return" with nothing (or falling off the end) returns None. Multiple values come back as a tuple: return a, b.

comfortable.body: Immediate exit through any enclosing finally blocks (which still run). Distinguish from yield: return ends, yield pauses.

gotcha: print shows a value; return gives it back. A function that only prints returns None.

novice.body: Inside a class, "self" means "this particular object." When you write self.name, you're reading or storing data that belongs to the specific object being used.

learning.body: The first parameter of a method — Python passes the instance in automatically when you call obj.method(). The name "self" is convention, not a keyword.

comfortable.body: Explicit instance receiver; obj.method(x) is sugar for Cls.method(obj, x). Forgetting it in the signature is the classic "takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given."

gotcha: self is not automatic *inside* the class body — every method must list it as the first parameter.

novice.body: Square brackets with a colon cut out a piece of a sequence: items[1:3] gives the items at positions 1 and 2. The stop position is not included.

learning.body: seq[start:stop:step] — any part can be omitted. Negative indexes count from the end, so seq[-2:] is the last two items and seq[::-1] is the sequence reversed.

comfortable.body: Half-open interval [start, stop) with optional stride; always returns a new object for lists, a view for memoryview/numpy.

gotcha: The stop index is excluded — seq[1:3] is two items, not three.

novice.body: A single star gathers or spreads a sequence. In a def, *args collects any number of extra arguments into a tuple; in a call, *mylist spreads a list out into separate arguments.

learning.body: Packing and unpacking: def f(*args) accepts variable arguments; f(*seq) unpacks one. Also works in assignment: first, *rest = items.

comfortable.body: Iterable packing/unpacking. In signatures, a bare * afterward forces keyword-only parameters.

gotcha: Inside the function, args is a plain tuple — the star exists only in the signature and call.

novice.body: Text in quotes. Single and double quotes mean the same thing; triple quotes let the text span multiple lines.

learning.body: Text in quotes; single, double, and triple-quoted forms are equivalent.

comfortable.body: String literal.

example.code:
message = "hello"
poem = """roses are red,
violets are blue"""

gotcha: Strings can't be changed in place — every "modification" builds a new string.

novice.body: try runs code that might fail; if a matching error happens, the except block handles it instead of crashing the program.

learning.body: Catch specific exception types — except ValueError — rather than everything. else runs when no exception occurred; finally runs no matter what.

comfortable.body: EAFP style: attempt and handle, rather than pre-check. Bare "except:" also swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit — almost never what you want.

gotcha: A bare except hides every error, including typos in your own code — always name the exception.

novice.body: The := sign assigns a value and uses it in the same expression — handy for "check something and keep the result" in one step.

learning.body: Assignment expression: "if (n := len(items)) > 10:" stores len(items) in n and tests it at once, so you don't compute it twice.

comfortable.body: Expression-level binding (PEP 572). Best in while-conditions and comprehension filters; anywhere else it usually costs more readability than it saves.

gotcha: It's an expression, not a statement — a bare "x := 5" line is a syntax error without parentheses.

novice.body: Repeats the indented block as long as the condition stays true. Something inside the loop must eventually change the condition, or it runs forever.

learning.body: Condition-driven repetition — use it when you don't know the number of passes in advance. break exits early; continue skips to the next check.

comfortable.body: Pre-test loop; "while True" with an internal break is the idiomatic loop-and-a-half for read-then-decide patterns.

gotcha: Forgetting to update the condition variable is the classic infinite loop.

novice.body: with opens something that needs cleanup — like a file — and guarantees it gets closed when the block ends, even if an error happens inside.

learning.body: Runs a block under a context manager: setup on entry, guaranteed teardown on exit. "as f" names whatever the manager hands you.

comfortable.body: Sugar for try/finally around __enter__/__exit__. Multiple managers can share one with; contextlib builds them from generators.

example.code:
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()

gotcha: The variable after "as" still exists after the block — but the resource behind it is already closed.
